title: Dockerizing an ML Inference Service
interviewAnswer: Package preprocessing, inference code and dependencies in an image. The model checkpoint can be baked into the image for simplicity or loaded from object storage/volume when versioning and image size matter.
why: Containerizing inference is a practical bridge from notebooks to reproducible deployment and is frequently expected in ML engineering interviews.
intuition: Docker packages code, runtime libraries and system dependencies into an immutable image. A container is a running instance of that image; model artifacts can be baked in or mounted/downloaded at runtime.
deepDive: Use a small trusted base image, pin dependencies, separate build/runtime stages, run as non-root, expose a clear entrypoint and keep secrets outside the image. Large/changing checkpoints are often stored in object/model storage and fetched by version; small fixed models can be copied into the image for simplicity. GPU containers require compatible host drivers/runtime, while CUDA libraries can live inside the image.
workedExample: Inference image contains Python, PyTorch, preprocessing code and API entrypoint; at startup it downloads model v12 from object storage, loads it once, then serves requests.
code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY src/ src/
CMD ["python","-m","src.server"]
commonMistakes: Storing passwords/API keys in the Dockerfile.
Re-downloading the model on every request instead of startup/cached load.
Assuming a Docker image includes a GPU driver independent of the host runtime.
followUps: Should the checkpoint be inside the image?
How would this run on AWS?
production: Push immutable tagged images to a registry, scan them, deploy by digest/version, emit health/metrics endpoints and keep model version separately traceable for rollback.
